hero.description: Chao Anouvong Park is where Vientiane’s monumental history meets everyday riverfront life: the large statue of King Anouvong faces the Mekong while joggers, families, vendors and evening market activity turn the space into a lived public park.
steps: Start at the King Anouvong statue
Walk south and north through the open park
Return as vendors begin setting up
Use the Mekong sunset as the endpoint
hero.rhythmNote: The park is weakest in the empty heat of midday and strongest when Vientiane starts using it. Come in late afternoon and stay long enough to see the public space change.

time.secondary: best folded into a longer riverfront evening

route.secondary: walkable from the central old-city area

budget.secondary: public park; food and shopping optional

chapters.label: THE MONUMENT
chapters.title: The king faces the river for a reason
chapters.body: The park is named for Chao Anouvong, the last king of the Vientiane Kingdom, and his large statue was installed in 2010. KPL describes the figure looking over the Mekong, giving the park a historical anchor that is easy to miss if you arrive only for the night market.

chapters.label: THE PARK
chapters.title: The real attraction arrives with local life
chapters.body: By late afternoon the riverbank fills with movement: walking, jogging, exercise, vendors and people sitting toward the Mekong. That daily use matters more than any fixed park itinerary. Walk through once, then let the atmosphere decide whether you stay for ten minutes or an hour.

note.label: ATLAS NOTE
note.text: Come for the statue, stay for the people. The evening public life is what stops Chao Anouvong Park from feeling like another formal monument.

chapters.label: URBAN CHANGE
chapters.title: This riverfront is a modern public-space project
chapters.body: KPL records the park as part of a larger Mekong riverside redevelopment and notes that it opened to the public in 2010. That recent history explains the broad, engineered promenade and why the area functions differently from the older temple streets nearby.

beforeYouLeave.title: Do not duplicate the Mekong Riverside Walk
beforeYouLeave.body: Use the park as one anchor within a broader riverfront evening. The separate riverside walk is the movement between places; Chao Anouvong Park is the pause where monument, exercise and market life concentrate.

note.label: BEST RHYTHM
note.text: Late afternoon into early evening gives the park its full transition.

items.label: Time needed
items.detail: Short if you only see the statue; longer when paired with sunset and the riverfront market.

items.label: Best time
items.detail: That is when the park becomes a real social space rather than an exposed daytime promenade.

items.label: Getting there
items.detail: Walkable from much of the old-city accommodation zone.

items.label: Cost
items.detail: The public park has no admission ticket; food, drinks and market purchases are optional.

faq.question: Who is the statue in Chao Anouvong Park?
faq.answer: It depicts Chao Anouvong, the last king of the Vientiane Kingdom. The statue was installed in 2010.

faq.question: When is the best time to visit the park?
faq.answer: Late afternoon and early evening, when joggers, families, vendors and riverfront activity give the space its real character.

faq.question: Is Chao Anouvong Park free?
faq.answer: Yes. It is a public riverfront park.

faq.question: How long do I need?
faq.answer: Thirty minutes is enough for the statue and a short walk, but an hour or more works better if you stay for sunset and evening activity.

faq.question: Is this the same as the Vientiane Night Market?
faq.answer: They overlap geographically in the riverfront experience, but the park itself is a public space and monument. Market stalls are one layer of the evening atmosphere rather than the whole reason to visit.
